newsitem.title: HONG KONG: No meeting of minds on Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: No meeting of minds on Hong Kong.

text.p: Talks between British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind and future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa failed on Sunday to narrow the gulf between the outgoing and incoming governments here.

With just 19 weeks to go until the British colony of Hong Kong returns to Chinas fold, the furore over Beijings plans to dismantle its legislature and roll back civil liberties laws have led to an ugly row in the wealthy community of six million people.

After his first meeting with Rifkind since his selection, Tung told reporters that London had refused to budge from its objections to Chinas plans to appoint an interim legislature and dilute various ordinances, including Hong Kongs bill of rights. Tung endorses such policies and Hong Kongs pro-democracy lobby vociferously opposes them.
Tung said he still harboured hopes that the British would relent and cooperate with Chinas provisional legislature.
"Britains position has always been clear, but I hope they will reconsider," said Tung, a billionaire shipping magnate who was anointed by Beijing in December.

Britain argues that the formation of the provisional legislature, which reverses the Patten reforms, is illegal under the terms of the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration. The pact binds Britain to restoring Hong Kong to China in mid-1997 and China to maintaining Hong Kongs freedoms and freewheeling capitalist way of life intact for 50 years.

Rifkind later lashed out at sceptics who say Britain is impotent against Chinas plans for Hong Kong after the handover at midnight on June 30, a date now 135 days away. He said Britain would exert maximum pressure on China to live up to the Joint Declaration and warned that the eys of the world were watching.
"The international dimension is not only a passive interest in Hong Kong but increasingly becoming an active interest particularly on the part of the United States," Rifkind said.
Rifkind, speaking later in a dinner speech, said that Londons responsibility did not end with the handover.
Britain, he said, would monitor events in its former colony and report to parliament every six month on Chinas promise to stick to its part of the Joint Declaration every six months.
"Hong Kong will remain Britains business for long after the handover. That is our wish and our pledge."

But in a palpable sign that British influence is waning fast after more than 150 years of colonial rule, only eight of Hong Kongs current legislatures made time to meet Rifkind on Sunday in a meeting brought forward from Monday.

Rifkinds visit, his second since taking up his post, was a whistlestop affair, cut short to let him return early to London for a key vote in Parliament on the "mad cow" crisis. A loss could trigger a vote of no confidence in the ruling Conservative Party, which is lagging in the polls in an election year.
Even five years ago, a meeting with the British foreign secretary would have been packed to the rafters, legislators said. Pro-Beijing legislator David Chu said the British were now irrelevent.

"The British government should face the reality to cooperate with China -- thats the most wise decision," Chu said in a statement titled "Good-bye, Rifkind!" faxed to the media a day before Rifkinds arrival on Saturday.
In the countdown to July 1, Hong Kong is awash with conflicting emotions which have pitted the pro-Beijing and pro-democracy camps against each other and sparked acrimonious exchanges.
Tung last week hit out at the Democracy Party, accusing it of blackening Hong Kongs name overseas by spreading doomsday predictions about the loss of freedoms.
He argued that Hong Kongs economy was buoyant, its people upbeat, and described Chinas plans as mere technicalities.

The pro-democracy camp described his statements as ominous. "This is just the beginning. The way things are going, Tung Chee-hwa and his government-in-waiting will be running out of popularity long before July 1," pro-democracy lawmaker Margaret Ng wrote in a newspaper column on Friday.

Another symbol of Hong Kongs British heritage passed into the history books during Rifkinds visit. The 115-year-old Royal Observatory, bestowed with its Royal prefix by King George V in 1912, dropped the royal coat of arms from its emblem.
Its new logo consists of spiralling cloudbanks, symbolising typhoons -- the fierce storms which periodically hit Hong Kong.
